positions/pre-nicene-logos-theology/oneL: The one God has from eternity his Word (Logos) and Wisdom, who comes forth as a distinct person to create, reveal and save — truly divine, but described as second in order.
positions/pre-nicene-logos-theology/core: The Father is the ultimate source (arche) of deity.
The Word is God's own reason, ‘begotten’ or ‘put forth’ for creation and revelation; the Spirit likewise.
Father, Son and Spirit are distinct in number but share one substance or power (Tertullian).
The Son mediates between the transcendent Father and the world; Old Testament theophanies are appearances of the Son.
positions/pre-nicene-logos-theology/orig: Developed by second-century Apologists (Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch, who first used trias c. 180), Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Origen, drawing on John's prologue, Jewish Wisdom literature and Middle Platonism.
positions/pre-nicene-logos-theology/stro: It allowed Christians to speak of Jesus as truly divine and personally distinct while keeping one source of deity.
It used the Bible's own Word and Wisdom categories and could explain to educated pagans how God relates to the world.
Tertullian's and Origen's vocabulary (substantia, persona, hypostasis, eternal generation) became the building blocks of later orthodoxy.
Its ranking language (‘second God’, ‘in the second place’) left the Son's full equality unclear and fed Arianism.
Some versions had the Word become a distinct person only for creation (‘two-stage’ Logos), implying the Son is not eternally Son.
Its Platonic mediator concept assumed the high God cannot touch the world directly — a premise Nicenes later rejected.
positions/pre-nicene-logos-theology/resp: Defenders note that ranking expressed order of origin, not inferiority of nature — the reading Nicenes later made explicit.
Origen already taught that there was no time when the Son was not, anticipating Nicaea.
positions/pre-nicene-logos-theology/cons: Provided both the vocabulary of Nicene orthodoxy and the premises of Arianism.
Shaped Christian apologetics in the Greco-Roman world.
positions/arianism/oneLine: The Son is the first and highest of God's works, created or begotten before time, through whom all else was made — divine by grace, not by nature equal to the unbegotten Father.
positions/arianism/coreClaims/0: God alone is unbegotten, without beginning, unchangeable; the Son, being begotten, has a beginning: ‘there was when he was not’.
positions/arianism/coreClaims/1: The Son was made ‘out of nothing’ by the Father's will, before all ages, and is the agent of creation.
positions/arianism/coreClaims/2: The Son is ‘God’ in a derivative sense and worthy of honour, but is not of the Father's essence.
positions/arianism/coreClaims/3: (Homoians, 359) The Son is ‘like the Father according to the Scriptures’; non-biblical terms like ousia should be banned. (Anomoeans) The Son is unlike the Father in essence, since ‘unbegotten’ defines God's essence.
positions/arianism/coreClaims/4: The Spirit is a creature of the Son.
positions/arianism/origin: Arius, presbyter of Baucalis in Alexandria, clashed with Bishop Alexander c. 318; he drew support from Eusebius of Nicomedia and others trained in the school of Lucian of Antioch. After Nicaea the movement fragmented into Homoians (Acacius, Ulfilas, Valens), Anomoeans (Aetius, Eunomius) and others.
positions/arianism/strongestArguments/0: It takes literally the biblical language of the Son's subordination, obedience, ignorance of the hour and prayer to the Father.
positions/arianism/strongestArguments/1: It protects the absolute uniqueness and impassibility of the unbegotten God, as the philosophical theology of the day demanded.
positions/arianism/strongestArguments/2: ‘Begotten’ naturally implies a beginning; a Son as old as his Father seemed incoherent.
positions/arianism/strongestArguments/3: Homoians argued that keeping to scriptural language avoided importing pagan metaphysics (ousia) into the creed.
positions/arianism/strongestObjections/0: Athanasius: Christians worship the Son and are baptised into his name; worshipping a creature is idolatry.
positions/arianism/strongestObjections/1: Only God can unite creatures to God; a created mediator cannot deify or save (On the Incarnation 54).
positions/arianism/strongestObjections/2: If the Father was once not Father, God changes — undermining the very immutability Arians wanted to protect.
positions/arianism/strongestObjections/3: John 1:1–3 says all things were made through the Word; if the Son was made, he made himself.
positions/arianism/strongestObjections/4: Proverbs 8:22 refers in context to Wisdom and, Athanasius argued, to the incarnate humanity.
positions/arianism/responses/0: Arians replied that worship of the Son is relative honour, given at the Father's command (Philippians 2:9–11; Hebrews 1:6).
positions/arianism/responses/1: Eunomius argued that clear thinking requires that ‘unbegotten’ names God's essence, so the begotten must differ in essence.
positions/arianism/responses/2: Homoians argued that the Nicene term was unbiblical and Sabellian, and won majorities at councils in 359–360.
positions/arianism/consequences/0: Sixty years of exiles, rival bishops and imperial interventions (325–381).
positions/arianism/consequences/1: Through Ulfilas, Homoian Christianity became the faith of the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians and Lombards; the Vandal persecution of Nicene Christians in North Africa (5th c.) and the conversion of Visigothic Spain (589) followed.
positions/arianism/consequences/2: ‘Arian’ remained a byword in later polemics; Isaac Newton, William Whiston and Samuel Clarke revived Arian-like views in the 18th century, and Jehovah's Witnesses today hold a Christology similar in structure (the Son as first creation).
positions/semi-arianism/oneLine: The Son is ‘like in essence’ (homoiousios) to the Father — truly God's Son by nature, yet distinct enough to avoid Sabellian confusion.
positions/semi-arianism/coreClaims/0: The Son is a true Son, sharing the Father's kind of being, not a creature made from nothing.
positions/semi-arianism/coreClaims/1: ‘Same essence’ (homoousios) risks merging Father and Son into one person (Sabellianism) or implying a material substance divided between them.
positions/semi-arianism/coreClaims/2: ‘Like in essence’ preserves both real sonship and real distinction.
positions/semi-arianism/coreClaims/3: Many held a cautious view of the Spirit (some became Pneumatomachians).
positions/semi-arianism/origin: A large conservative Eastern party, articulated by Basil of Ancyra and George of Laodicea at the Synod of Ancyra (358), reacting against the radical Anomoeans.
positions/semi-arianism/strongestArgumen: It firmly rejected Arius' creaturely Son while answering real fears that homoousios was modalist (the word had been rejected at Antioch in 268).
Its formula seemed closer to biblical images (image, radiance) of the Son's likeness to the Father.
It represented the actual majority of Eastern bishops in the 350s.
positions/semi-arianism/strongestObjecti: Athanasius argued that ‘likeness’ applies to qualities, not essences; if the Son is only like God, he is not God.
The formula could not exclude Homoians, who also said ‘like’, and so failed to stop Arian drift.
Two essences that are merely similar imply two gods.
positions/semi-arianism/responses/0: Athanasius (De Synodis, 359) recognised the Homoiousians as ‘brothers’ who meant what Nicaea meant, opening reconciliation.
positions/semi-arianism/responses/1: The Cappadocians, partly from this milieu, showed that homoousios could be read without Sabellianism by distinguishing ousia and hypostasis.
positions/semi-arianism/consequences/0: Its alliance with Athanasius and the Cappadocians created the coalition that triumphed at Constantinople (381).
positions/semi-arianism/consequences/1: The pejorative label ‘Semi-Arian’ (from Epiphanius) obscured for centuries how anti-Arian this party was.
positions/pneumatomachianism/oneLine: The Son is of the Father's essence (or like it), but the Holy Spirit is a ministering power or the highest of creatures, not God.
positions/pneumatomachianism/coreClaims/: Scripture never explicitly calls the Spirit ‘God’ or commands prayer to the Spirit.
The Spirit is a servant sent by Father and Son, of a rank between God and creatures.
Glory should be given to the Father through the Son in the Spirit, not ‘with’ the Spirit.
positions/pneumatomachianism/origin: Emerged c. 360 in Egypt (the Tropici, answered in Athanasius' Letters to Serapion) and in Asia Minor around Eustathius of Sebaste; named after Macedonius of Constantinople.
positions/pneumatomachianism/strongestAr: The New Testament's explicit language about the Spirit's deity is sparse compared with that about the Son.
The Spirit is consistently ‘sent’ and ‘given’, suggesting a subordinate role.
Cautious biblicism: they would not confess more than Scripture plainly said.
positions/pneumatomachianism/strongestOb: The Spirit is included in the one baptismal name (Matthew 28:19) and lying to the Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3–4).
The Spirit sanctifies and deifies; only God can make holy (Athanasius, Letters to Serapion; Basil, On the Holy Spirit).
If the Spirit were a creature, baptism would be into a creature.
positions/pneumatomachianism/responses/0: Pneumatomachians replied that inclusion in a formula shows association, not identity of nature.
positions/pneumatomachianism/responses/1: Gregory of Nazianzus answered that revelation is progressive: the Spirit's deity is ‘suggested’ in the New Testament and clarified by the Spirit's own presence in the Church.
positions/pneumatomachianism/consequence: Produced Basil's On the Holy Spirit and Gregory's Fifth Theological Oration.
Condemned at Constantinople (381), whose creed expanded the article on the Spirit.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/oneLine: The Son is ‘God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten not made, of one essence (homoousios) with the Father’; the Spirit is worshipped and glorified with them.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/coreClaims/0: The Son is eternally begotten of the Father's own essence, not created; there was never a time when the Father was without the Son.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/coreClaims/1: Father and Son are homoousios — the same in deity, distinct in that one begets and the other is begotten.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/coreClaims/2: The Holy Spirit is Lord and Giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshipped and glorified together with Father and Son (381).
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/coreClaims/3: The incarnation of the true God is necessary for salvation: only God can restore the image of God and give incorruption.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/origin: Defined at the Council of Nicaea (325) against Arius, championed by Alexander and Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra and Western bishops (Hilary of Poitiers, Ossius of Córdoba), and reaffirmed with the Spirit article at Constantinople (381).
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/strongestArgu: It alone fits the New Testament's worship of Jesus and the application to him of YHWH texts (e.g. Philippians 2:10–11 / Isaiah 45:23; John 12:41 / Isaiah 6).
Soteriological argument: only true God incarnate can unite humanity to God (‘He was made man that we might be made God’).
It preserves real distinction (against modalism) and real unity (against Arian ditheism or polytheism).
It has been the shared confession of nearly all churches for 1,600 years, across Greek, Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Ge'ez and modern languages.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/strongestObje: The key term homoousios is not in Scripture and had been rejected at Antioch (268); critics call it the Hellenisation of the gospel (Harnack).
It was enforced by imperial power, which raises questions about whether it was truly the church's free consensus.
Unitarians and others argue that ‘three persons, one God’ is logically incoherent or unintelligible.
Texts of the Son's subordination and ignorance (Mark 13:32; John 14:28; 1 Corinthians 15:28) seem to be explained away.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/responses/0: Nicenes reply that a non-biblical word was needed precisely because Arians could agree to every biblical phrase while meaning something else.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/responses/1: Imperial power backed Arians and Homoians as often as Nicenes (under Constantius II and Valens); Nicaea prevailed through argument and broad reception, not only force.
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/responses/2: The doctrine claims to be a grammar safeguarding mystery, not a mathematical claim; ‘one’ and ‘three’ refer to different things (essence, hypostasis).
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/responses/3: Subordination texts are read of the incarnate Son's humanity or of the Son's eternal origin (order, not inferiority).
positions/nicene-orthodoxy/consequences/: Produced the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, recited in the liturgy of most churches worldwide.
Established the model of ecumenical councils as means of settling doctrine — and of imperial involvement in doctrine.
Became the boundary marker distinguishing historic Christian bodies from nontrinitarian movements.
